solution.concept_anchor: Carry bag thickness norms — 75 microns in 2021, 120 microns target
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall that the original PWMR 2016 set a 50-micron threshold may select (a), confusing the original norm with the 2021 amendment's revised norm.
elimination_logic: The question focuses on the thickness threshold in the 2021 amendment — not the original 2016 norm.
The original PWMR 2016 set 50 microns as the minimum thickness for carry bags.
The 2021 amendment raised this to 75 microns with a further target of 120 microns.
Option (b) correctly states 75 microns as the 2021 threshold, with 120 microns as the subsequent target.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The three threshold numbers — 50 microns (original 2016), 75 microns (2021 amendment), and 120 microns (2022 target) — create an ideal temporal-swap trap. Students who have studied PWMR know thickness norms exist but frequently confuse which norm applies at which amendment. The 50-micron figure, being the original and most widely circulated number in pre-2021 study material, is the most powerful wrong attractor.
solution.final_explanation:
The thickness thresholds for plastic carry bags have been progressively raised to phase out thinner, harder-to-recycle bags.

• Option (a): Incorrect — 50 microns was the threshold under the original PWMR 2016, not the 2021 amendment.
• Option (b): Correct — the 2021 amendment raised the minimum carry bag thickness from 50 microns to 75 microns, with a further target of 120 microns by end of 2022. This progressive approach aims to incentivise thicker, more recyclable bags.
• Option (c): Incorrect — 100 microns was never the specified threshold under any PWMR amendment; this is a plausible but fabricated number.
• Option (d): Incorrect — 120 microns is the further target under the 2022 timeline, not the threshold set by the 2021 amendment itself.

Value Addition:
• The thickness increase serves two purposes: thicker bags are more durable (encouraging reuse) and more economically viable for recycling.
• Non-woven polypropylene bags below 60 GSM were simultaneously banned by the 2021 amendment.
• Carry bags made from recycled plastic are subject to different colour and composition norms under PWMR.

solution.concept_anchor: Ghost gear contribution to GPGP — 46% by weight
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may recall the headline figure of plastics in the GPGP without knowing the specific composition breakdown — option (a) seems plausible as a generic plastic pollution statistic.
elimination_logic: Test option (a): 80% of marine plastic from land sources is correct, but attributing this to 'ship-to-shore discharge' reverses the direction — land sources means plastic flows FROM land TO ocean via rivers, not from ships to shore.

Test option (b): plastic pollution is recognised as a planetary boundary concern, but it is NOT yet a standalone target in the CBD Kunming-Montreal Framework — this is a partial-truth (it is cited as a threat but not a standalone CBD target).
Test option (c): ghost fishing gear constituting ~46% of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch by weight is the correctly matched pair from the key dimensions.
Test option (d): microplastic ingestion by zooplankton disrupts the carbon pump — but the claim that 'plastic debris enhances' it is incorrect; it disrupts/reduces efficiency.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) deploys a reversed-causation/geographic-swap combination: '80% of marine plastic from ship-to-shore discharge' sounds like a plausible marine pollution statistic but reverses the actual pathway (land-to-ocean via rivers = 80%). Students who recall the 80% figure without internalising the direction of the pathway will select (a) as correctly matched.
solution.final_explanation:
Marine plastic pollution involves several well-quantified facts that are frequently tested with slight distortions.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched — 80% of marine plastic originates from land-based sources (rivers, coastal dumping, stormwater), NOT from ship-to-shore discharge. This statement reverses the pathway.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched — plastic pollution is cited as one of the three planetary boundary crises, but it is NOT formally integrated as a standalone target in the CBD Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022). It is acknowledged as a threat within other targets but lacks a dedicated standalone target.
• Option (c): Correctly matched — ghost fishing gear (derelict nets, traps, lines) constitutes approximately 46% of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch by weight, making it the single largest component by mass.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched — microplastic ingestion by zooplankton DISRUPTS (reduces efficiency of) the biological carbon pump, not enhances it. Disrupted feeding reduces the density of fecal pellets that sink carbon to the deep ocean.

Value Addition:
• Ghost gear poses severe entanglement risks to sea turtles, cetaceans, and seabirds.
• KAZA (Kunming-Kunming-Montreal) GBF's 30x30 target addresses habitat protection but does not specifically mention plastic pollution.
• The biological carbon pump is a key mechanism for ocean carbon sequestration — its disruption has climate feedback implications.

solution.concept_anchor: Plastics GHG contribution — 3.4% global emissions; black carbon from burning

statement_analysis.statement: Approximately 90% of plastics are synthesised from virgin petrochemical feedstocks, and plastic production across the full lifecycle contributes roughly 3.4% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
statement_analysis.reason: The vast majority of plastics are derived from fossil fuel feedstocks (oil, natural gas); lifecycle GHG assessments place plastic production at approximately 3.4% of global emissions.

statement_analysis.statement: Open burning of plastic waste, which is common in India's informal waste management sector, releases black carbon — a short-lived climate forcer whose near-term warming impact per unit mass exceeds that of carbon dioxide.
statement_analysis.reason: Open burning of mixed plastic waste produces black carbon (soot), which has a global warming potential far exceeding CO2 over a 20-year horizon, making it disproportionately impactful in the short term.

statement_analysis.statement: Mechanical recycling of plastic is a fully circular solution because it preserves the original polymer quality through multiple recycling cycles, eliminating the need for virgin feedstock input over time.
statement_analysis.reason: Mechanical recycling causes polymer chain degradation (downcycling), limiting most plastics to 1–2 recycling cycles before quality becomes unacceptable. It is not a fully circular solution and cannot eliminate virgin feedstock demand.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who view mechanical recycling as environmentally virtuous may assume Statement 3 is also correct and choose (d) for all three statements.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: 90% petrochemical origin and 3.4% GHG contribution are cited figures — correct.
Confirm Statement 2: black carbon from open burning exceeds CO2 in short-term warming impact per unit — correct.

Scrutinise Statement 3: 'fully circular' and 'eliminating need for virgin feedstock' are scope-extension qualifiers — mechanical recycling downcycles polymer quality; it is not a zero-virgin-input solution after 1–2 cycles.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses 'fully circular' and 'eliminating the need for virgin feedstock over time' — both qualifiers that extend the actual benefit of mechanical recycling beyond what the evidence supports. Mechanical recycling is beneficial compared to disposal, but polymer degradation means the material cannot be endlessly recycled. Students who have read about the circular economy may assume recycling = circular = no virgin input needed, falling for the scope-extension trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Plastics' climate impact operates across its full lifecycle, from fossil fuel extraction through to end-of-life treatment.

• Statement 1 — Correct: ~90% of plastics use virgin petrochemical feedstocks; full lifecycle GHG contribution is approximately 3.4% of global emissions — a significant sectoral share.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Open burning of plastic waste generates black carbon (soot), which has a global warming potential 460–1,500 times that of CO2 over 20 years. India's widespread open burning of mixed plastic waste is therefore a disproportionate near-term climate concern.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Mechanical recycling degrades polymer chains — a process called downcycling. Most plastics can only be mechanically recycled 1–2 times before the material quality becomes unsuitable for the original application. Virgin feedstock input cannot be eliminated through mechanical recycling alone.

Value Addition:
• Chemical recycling (pyrolysis) is promoted as a solution to mechanical recycling's downcycling problem but is energy-intensive and produces toxic by-products.
• Dioxins and furans from plastic open burning are persistent organic pollutants regulated under the Stockholm Convention.
• Black carbon reduction is one of the fastest ways to achieve near-term climate benefits — addressing plastic open burning in India has co-benefits for both air quality and climate.

solution.concept_anchor: NGT suo motu powers under NGT Act 2010 for PWMR enforcement
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may reason that 'because NGT can enforce PWMR (R), it can take suo motu cognizance of plastic pollution (A)' — treating the enforcement power as causing the suo motu power, which conflates two distinct NGT powers.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? NGT has taken suo motu cognizance of plastic pollution cases — yes, this is factually established under NGT practice.
Step 2: Is R correct? NGT Act 2010 does empower NGT to enforce violations of environmental laws including PWMR — yes, R is correct.

Step 3: Does R explain A? The suo motu power derives from Section 14 of the NGT Act (original jurisdiction over substantial environmental questions), not from PWMR enforcement power per se. Enforcement power and suo motu jurisdiction are distinct powers of NGT — R's enforcement power does not causally produce A's suo motu cognizance authority.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both assertions are factually accurate NGT powers — it can enforce PWMR and it does take suo motu cognizance of environmental issues. The trap is in the causal direction: students may reason that because NGT can enforce PWMR (R), it therefore takes suo motu cognizance of plastic cases (A). But NGT's suo motu jurisdiction derives from its original jurisdiction under Section 14 of the NGT Act 2010, not from any specific enforcement power under PWMR. These are independent statutory powers — R does not cause or explain A.
solution.final_explanation:
The National Green Tribunal (NGT Act 2010) has two relevant but distinct powers at play here.

Assertion (A): Correct. NGT has exercised suo motu jurisdiction in plastic pollution matters — taking up cases based on media reports and petitions without a formal complaint from affected parties. This suo motu power flows from NGT's original jurisdiction under Section 14 of the NGT Act over 'substantial questions relating to the environment.'

Reason (R): Correct. NGT is empowered to enforce violations of environmental laws listed in the NGT Act's Schedule — this includes the Environment Protection Act 1986, under which PWMR is notified. NGT can therefore issue directions, impose penalties, and monitor PWMR compliance.

Causal relationship: R is true and relevant context, but it does not explain A. The suo motu power is an independent grant of jurisdiction under the NGT Act, not a consequence of PWMR enforcement authority. Both powers exist separately in the NGT Act.

Value Addition:
• NGT has jurisdiction over civil cases involving substantial environmental questions arising from the seven scheduled environmental laws including EPA 1986 and Water Act 1974.
• States can enact stricter plastic bans than central PWMR; NGT can enforce both central and state environmental legislation.
• Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (FD) provide the constitutional anchor for all environmental legislation including PWMR.

solution.concept_anchor: EPR categories 2022 — four packaging types with separate targets

statement_analysis.statement: Under India's EPR Guidelines for plastic packaging (2022), all plastic packaging is treated as a single homogeneous category with uniform collection and recycling targets applicable to all producers, importers, and brand owners.
statement_analysis.reason: EPR Guidelines 2022 created four distinct categories — rigid plastic packaging, flexible plastic packaging, multilayer packaging, and compostable plastic packaging — each with separate and differentiated targets. There is no single uniform target.

statement_analysis.statement: SEBI's ESG disclosure framework requires large listed companies to report data on plastic waste generated and recycled, creating a corporate governance interface with India's plastic waste regulation.
statement_analysis.reason: SEBI has integrated plastic waste reporting into its ESG disclosure requirements for large listed companies — this is a factually accurate connection between corporate governance and plastic waste management.

statement_analysis.statement: The risk of double counting in India's plastic credit system arises when the same plastic waste recovery is claimed simultaneously under both a voluntary plastic credit scheme and a mandatory EPR certificate, allowing the same environmental benefit to be counted twice.
statement_analysis.reason: Double counting is a documented governance risk in India's EPR framework — the same physical plastic waste recovery could theoretically be used to generate voluntary market credits AND mandatory EPR certificates, inflating the apparent environmental benefit.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who have not studied the detailed EPR guidelines may assume a single uniform target is administratively simpler and therefore likely, marking Statement 1 as correct and confusing it with Statement 2 or 3.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: EPR Guidelines 2022 have four separate categories with differentiated targets — a single uniform category does NOT exist. Statement 1 is the incorrect one.
Test Statement 2: SEBI ESG framework does require plastic waste reporting for large listed companies — correct, not incorrect.
Test Statement 3: double counting risk is explicitly documented in EPR credit trading literature — correct, not incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap here assumes administrative simplicity — a uniform single target across all plastic packaging types sounds like reasonable regulation. The actual EPR Guidelines 2022 created four distinct packaging categories because their recycling economics, material properties, and waste management pathways are fundamentally different. Multilayer packaging (nearly impossible to recycle mechanically) cannot have the same targets as rigid PET bottles (high recycling value). A student who has not read the guidelines in detail will assume a single category.
solution.final_explanation:
India's EPR Guidelines for plastic packaging (2022) represent a significant step up in regulatory sophistication from the original PWMR 2016.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 2022 EPR Guidelines created four separate packaging categories: (i) rigid plastic packaging, (ii) flexible plastic packaging, (iii) multilayer packaging, and (iv) compostable plastic packaging — each with differentiated collection, recycling, and end-of-use targets reflecting different material properties and recycling economics.
• Statement 2 — Correct: SEBI's ESG disclosure requirements (BRSR framework) for top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation include reporting on plastic waste generated and recycled, creating a governance linkage between capital markets and plastic waste compliance.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Double counting is a documented risk — the same physical plastic recovery could generate both voluntary market credits (Verra) and mandatory EPR certificates, inflating apparent environmental compliance without additional real-world impact.

Value Addition:
• Compostable plastic packaging, despite having its own EPR category, must still carry BIS certification under IS/ISO 17088.
• EPR non-compliance can trigger action under EPA 1986, with penalties including closure of manufacturing operations.
• The centralised EPR portal is administered by CPCB and requires all PIBOs to register and submit annual compliance reports.

solution.concept_anchor: EPR formalisation vs. waste picker marginalisation
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know NGT has broad environmental enforcement powers may suggest it should mandate a co-processing solution, confusing a technically viable option with the policy-correct intervention.
elimination_logic: Identify the core policy tension: EPR formalisation through certificate trading excludes informal waste pickers who lack legal registration and institutional capacity.
The scenario asks what policy intervention best addresses waste picker exclusion from the EPR credit system.
Option (a) directly addresses the structural exclusion by integrating waste pickers into the EPR credit framework — consistent with ILO/UNEP recommendations and PWMR's acknowledgement of their role.
Eliminate (b): restricting EPR compliance to cement kilns replaces the recycling market entirely — it does not address waste picker inclusion.
Eliminate (c): NGT mandating co-processing is a disposal solution, not an inclusion solution for waste pickers.
Eliminate (d): extending SBM to cover EPR compliance ignores the jurisdictional distinction — SBM does not have plastic recycling targets.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates through option (d), which sounds reasonable — SBM is India's flagship cleanliness mission, so extending it to cover plastic recycling seems like a logical administrative step. But SBM's mandate is explicitly ODF and sanitation — it does not have the regulatory architecture for EPR compliance or waste picker integration. Expanding SBM beyond its mandate would require legislative changes, not a policy notification.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the governance challenge of integrating India's informal plastic recycling workforce into a formalising EPR system.

• Option (a): Correct. Providing waste pickers with access to the EPR certificate trading system — through cooperative models, aggregators, or direct registration pathways — directly addresses the structural exclusion. This approach is endorsed by ILO, UNEP, and is consistent with PWMR's acknowledgement of waste pickers as key actors. Formalisation without inclusion defeats the purpose of building on India's existing recycling infrastructure.
• Option (b): Incorrect — limiting EPR compliance to cement kiln co-processing eliminates the recycling market entirely and would displace waste pickers from their livelihoods, worsening exclusion.
• Option (c): Incorrect — NGT mandating co-processing is a valid enforcement tool for a different problem (waste disposal), not a solution to waste picker inclusion in EPR credit trading.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Swachh Bharat Mission lacks a dedicated plastic recycling mandate or EPR compliance framework; extending it to cover EPR would require fundamental restructuring beyond its current statutory scope.

Value Addition:
• Waste picker cooperatives (e.g., SWaCH in Pune) demonstrate models for integrating informal workers into formal waste management systems.
• ILO's Decent Work agenda specifically covers waste pickers under informal economy frameworks.
• India's informal recycling sector processes ~60% of plastic waste — any EPR system that marginalises this sector risks reducing overall recycling rates.

statement_analysis.statement: PVC (Resin Code 3) is recyclable in principle but presents processing challenges due to its chlorine content and toxic additives such as phthalate plasticisers and lead stabilisers.
statement_analysis.reason: PVC can technically be recycled but its chlorine-based chemistry and common additives (phthalates, heavy metal stabilisers) create significant environmental and health hazards during reprocessing, limiting its practical recyclability.

statement_analysis.reason: Expanded polystyrene (thermocol) for decoration and packaging, and polystyrene cups and plates, are specifically listed among the 19 banned single-use plastic items under PWMR Amendment Rules 2021.

statement_analysis.statement: Multilayer plastic packaging, which typically carries Resin Code 7, was banned outright by the PWMR 2021 amendment alongside the 19 single-use plastic items because it is non-recyclable.
statement_analysis.reason: Multilayer plastic packaging is NOT banned outright by PWMR 2021 — it is subject to EPR obligations and was targeted for phased elimination under the 2018 amendment, but remains in use and in the EPR framework.

statement_analysis.statement: LDPE (Resin Code 4) is commonly used for plastic carry bags; carry bags made from LDPE below the prescribed thickness threshold (75 microns) were prohibited under the PWMR 2021 amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: LDPE is a primary material for plastic carry bags; PWMR 2021 raised the minimum thickness for carry bags to 75 microns, effectively banning LDPE carry bags below this thickness threshold.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who associate multilayer plastic with 'banned' because of the 2018 amendment's phased elimination language may count all four as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — PVC recyclability limitations due to chlorine and additives are established.
Statement 2 is correct — thermocol cups and polystyrene items are in the 19-item ban list.
Statement 3 is the trap: multilayer packaging is subject to EPR, not outright banned by PWMR 2021 — incorrect.
Statement 4 is correct — LDPE carry bags below 75 microns banned under 2021 amendment.
Three statements correct — select option (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 2018 amendment called for 'phased elimination' of non-recyclable multilayer plastic, and students who read this as an 'outright ban' will incorrectly mark Statement 3 as correct. The 2021 amendment did not ban multilayer packaging — it placed it under EPR with specific targets. The conflation of 'phased elimination direction' (2018) with 'outright ban' (not enacted for MLP) is the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precise knowledge across both the resin identification system and the specific banned versus EPR-regulated categories under PWMR 2021.

• Statement 1 — Correct: PVC (Code 3) has theoretical recyclability but is problematic due to chlorine content (generating dioxins if burned), phthalate plasticisers, and lead/cadmium stabilisers.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Thermocol (EPS) for decoration, cups, and plates appears explicitly in India's 19-item SUP ban list under PWMR 2021.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Multilayer packaging (Code 7) was targeted for phased elimination under the 2018 amendment and placed under EPR in 2022 — it was NOT included in the 19 outright-banned items under PWMR 2021.
• Statement 4 — Correct: LDPE carry bags (Code 4) below 75 microns are prohibited under the 2021 amendment's revised thickness norm.

Value Addition:
• The 2018 PWMR amendment set a phase-out timeline for non-recyclable, non-energy-recoverable multilayer plastics — the timeline has faced compliance challenges.
• Code 7 includes diverse materials: polycarbonate (BPA source), bioplastics (PLA, PHA), nylon, and multilayer laminates — all with very different environmental profiles.
• EPR targets for multilayer packaging are more stringent than for rigid or flexible single-layer packaging.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: Microplastics have been detected in the Ganga and Yamuna rivers as well as in Chilika Lake, and IUCN Red List species inhabiting these ecosystems face a compounded threat from both plastic ingestion and habitat degradation.
statement_analysis.reason: Microplastics have been scientifically documented in the Ganga, Yamuna, and Chilika Lake. These ecosystems host multiple IUCN Red List species (Ganges river dolphin, Irrawaddy dolphin in Chilika), which face dual threats from plastic ingestion and habitat loss.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: India has established permissible limits for microplastic concentrations in freshwater under its National Water Quality Standards, and CPCB monitors microplastic levels in rivers as part of its routine water quality surveillance.
statement_analysis.reason: India has no established permissible limits for microplastics in freshwater under BIS or National Water Quality Standards, and CPCB's routine monitoring does not currently include standardised microplastic surveillance — this is a documented regulatory and monitoring gap.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students aware that CPCB monitors river water quality may assume that a monitoring infrastructure for microplastics already exists, marking Statement 2 as correct.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: microplastic detection in Ganga, Yamuna, Chilika and the IUCN Red List species dual threat are documented facts — Statement 1 is correct.

Scrutinise Statement 2: India lacks permissible limits for microplastics in freshwater and CPCB's current routine monitoring does not include standardised microplastic parameters — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: CPCB's extensive river monitoring network (monitoring hundreds of stations across India) makes it natural to assume that microplastic monitoring is included. The scope-extension trap works by assuming that because CPCB monitors water quality comprehensively, it must monitor all pollution parameters including microplastics. India's microplastic monitoring gap is a specific and important regulatory fact — permissible limits and routine surveillance both remain absent.
solution.final_explanation:
Freshwater ecosystems in India face a double environmental burden from plastic pollution — microplastics in water bodies and the resulting biological impacts on endemic species.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Scientific studies have documented microplastics in the Ganga, Yamuna, and Chilika Lake. Species like the Gangetic river dolphin (Platanista gangetica, Endangered) and Irrawaddy dolphins (Chilika Lake) face dual threats: plastic ingestion and the broader habitat degradation from pollution and human activity.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: India has not established any permissible limit for microplastics in freshwater under BIS standards or National Water Quality Standards. CPCB's routine water quality monitoring network — though extensive — does not currently include standardised microplastic parameters. This is an explicitly identified regulatory and monitoring gap.

Value Addition:
• WHO's 2022 microplastics report called on governments to establish monitoring frameworks and standards — India has not yet responded with regulatory action.
• The Gangetic river dolphin is India's National Aquatic Animal and is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List.
• Chilika Lake is India's largest coastal lagoon and a Ramsar site — microplastic contamination here has implications for fisheries-dependent communities.

solution.concept_anchor: India plastic waste generation — 3.5 MT, 40% uncollected, per capita vs. absolute

statement_analysis.statement: India generates approximately 3.5 million tonnes of plastic waste annually, of which around 40% remains uncollected and is susceptible to open burning or open dumping.
statement_analysis.reason: CPCB data indicates India generates ~3.5 million tonnes of plastic waste annually, with approximately 40% remaining uncollected — entering open environments through burning, dumping, or littering.

statement_analysis.statement: India's per capita plastic waste generation exceeds that of most OECD nations, explaining why its absolute contribution to global plastic pollution is so large.
statement_analysis.reason: India's per capita plastic waste generation is significantly lower than that of OECD nations. India's large absolute volume results from its massive population size, not per capita excess.

statement_analysis.statement: 'Plastic Overshoot Day,' as used by EA Earth Action, refers to the date in a year when a country's plastic waste generation exceeds the capacity of its waste management infrastructure to process it adequately.
statement_analysis.reason: Plastic Overshoot Day (by EA Earth Action) is defined as the point when plastic waste generation outpaces the country's waste management infrastructure capacity — India crosses this threshold early in the calendar year due to infrastructure deficits.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who conflate 'large absolute volume' with 'high per capita generation' may mark Statement 2 as correct and choose (d) for all three.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: 3.5 million tonnes annually and 40% uncollected are CPCB-cited figures — correct.

Identify the trap in Statement 2: India's per capita plastic consumption is LOWER than OECD nations (India ~11 kg/person/year vs. 100+ kg in USA) — the large absolute number is purely a function of population size, not per capita excess.
Confirm Statement 3: Plastic Overshoot Day definition matches the EA Earth Action methodology — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 conflates two distinct metrics: absolute volume and per capita generation. In discussions of India's plastic pollution, these are frequently blurred — large absolute numbers give the impression of high per capita consumption when in fact India's per capita plastic consumption is one of the lowest among major economies. This conflation is a standard distractor in questions about India's environmental performance metrics.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding India's plastic pollution profile requires distinguishing between per capita and absolute metrics.

• Statement 1 — Correct: India generates ~3.5 million tonnes of plastic waste annually; ~40% remains uncollected, entering open environments through burning or dumping — the primary source of both air and land pollution.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: India's per capita plastic waste generation (~11 kg/person/year) is substantially lower than OECD nations (USA: ~130 kg, EU average: ~35 kg). India's large absolute volume is a consequence of its 1.4 billion population, not high per capita consumption.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Plastic Overshoot Day (EA Earth Action) marks when a country's plastic waste outpaces its management infrastructure capacity. India crosses this threshold early due to collection and processing infrastructure deficits relative to generation volume.

Value Addition:
• The Mismanaged Plastic Waste Index ranks countries by proportion of plastic that is improperly handled — India ranks poorly despite low per capita generation.
• Improving India's waste collection infrastructure from 60% to 90% would dramatically reduce both the Mismanaged Plastic index and open burning emissions.
• Per capita data is essential to interpret any country-level plastic pollution statistic accurately.

solution.final_explanation:
This question tests simultaneous knowledge of multiple plastic regulatory distinctions.

• Option (a): Correctly matched. Oxo-degradable plastics contain pro-oxidant additives that accelerate fragmentation into microplastics — they are explicitly banned under PWMR 2021 precisely because fragmentation does NOT equal biodegradation.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched. Cotton bags require approximately 7,100 uses (not 50) to offset the carbon footprint of one conventional plastic bag, based on LCA studies accounting for water-intensive cotton cultivation.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched. Compostable plastics certified under IS/ISO 17088 are permitted but are NOT exempt from EPR obligations — they form one of four separate packaging categories under EPR Guidelines 2022.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. Chemical migration limits for food-contact plastics fall under FSSAI's mandate (Food Safety and Standards Act 2006), not MoEFCC's PWMR — though both regulatory bodies have overlapping interests in this area.

Value Addition:
• The four EPR packaging categories: rigid, flexible, multilayer, compostable — each with differentiated targets.
• Oxo-degradable and photodegradable plastics are both banned under PWMR 2021 for the same reason: microplastic fragmentation.
• BIS certification under IS/ISO 17088 is a prerequisite for any plastic claiming compostability in India.
